Manifest Destiny. The nineteenth-century American ideology that the United States was divinely ordained to expand across the North American continent from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean. This belief justified territorial conquest, Indian removal, and aggressive expansionism, shaping American foreign policy and dramatically altering the geopolitical landscape, though it resulted in the displacement and suffering of indigenous populations.

The term Manifest Destiny was coined in eighteen forty-five to articulate a belief held by many Americans that territorial expansion was inevitable, justified, and morally right. The ideology drew on Protestant eschatology, nationalist fervor, and pseudoscientific racial theories claiming Anglo-Saxon or Anglo-American racial superiority, framing expansion as a civilizing and Christian mission. Manifest Destiny motivated the Louisiana Purchase in eighteen hundred and three, territorial acquisition from Spain including Florida and Texas, the Mexican-American War from eighteen forty-six to eighteen forty-eight which seized the Southwest, and the Oregon Treaty in eighteen forty-six with Britain.

The expansion came at catastrophic cost to Native American peoples. The Indian Removal Act of eighteen thirty, the Trail of Tears, forced relocations, broken treaties, and genocidal warfare displaced millions from their ancestral lands. Manifest Destiny exacerbated sectional tensions over slavery. Each new territory prompted conflicts over whether slavery would be permitted, driving the country toward civil war.

The ideology extended internationally. American imperialists applied Manifest Destiny logic to justify interventions in Latin America and the Pacific, including the Spanish-American War in eighteen ninety-eight and subsequent colonial acquisitions. Modern scholars critique Manifest Destiny as a retrospective rationalization for colonialism and genocide, though the ideology deeply shaped American self-identity and territorial ambitions for generations. Manifest Destiny shaped American territorial development and identity, connects to the Louisiana Purchase, the largest territorial acquisition justified by expansionist ideology, to Native Americans, indigenous peoples displaced and destroyed by American expansionism, to the Mexican-American War, conflict driven by territorial ambitions and Manifest Destiny ideology, and to slavery, whose sectional conflict over expansion into new territories would tear the nation apart.
